agent_notes: Applied the reviewer request: the מֵאַיִן note now cites Jacob's question to the shepherds of Haran (Gen 29:4), not Joseph's brothers. The verse is a question, so I read אֶשָּׂא as a plain present 'I lift up' (YLT, BBE) rather than KJV/ASV 'I will lift up'.

Whether the mountains are a source of help (hills with shrines, or hills from which rescuers might appear) or a threat (bandits, high places) is disputed. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David read the speaker as a watcher scanning the heights for helpers; I follow that and keep the dramatic layer open to the question. The 'high places' reading is my own and is marked as such in the commentary.

agent_notes: Applied the reviewer request: the literal layer keeps the jussive ('May he not give…'), and the commentary presents the wish as one reading of the form, noting Ibn Ezra (אל = לא) and the Targum (לָא) behind the KJV 'will not'. STEPBible glosses 'he permit'; I corrected it to 'may he not give' for the pair of אַל words, with לַמּוֹט glossed as 'to the slipping' (a noun, 'stumbling').

The dramatic layer shifts from the speaker's 'I' in verse 1 to a second-person voice ('your foot'). The text does not say who speaks; Malbim hears a voice answering the speaker, Radak and Meiri one person comforting another. I leave the speaker unnamed.

agent_notes: The Hebrew verb יַכֶּכָּה is the same 'strike' verb used of sunstroke in 2 Kings 4:18-20 and Isa 49:10; I did not use those parallels as a source because the packet does not give them, but the sense of sunstroke is the common one. The moon's harm is attested in the commentaries only as medieval theory about moisture (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David); I flag that as the commentators' world, not as established ancient belief.
